summary:
Penang stands under the national framework of Malaysia: the federal Penal Code offences covering "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and "gross indecency" apply in the state, and no Penang-specific exemption, provision or protective statute is recorded. A visitor's exposure in Penang is set by that national framework together with the state's own Sharia enactment.

Penang is one of the 13 Malaysian states that criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity for Muslims through a Sharia enactment. The enactment bars Muslim men from dressing as women and carries penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a RM5,000 fine and up to six strokes of the cane. Enforcement rests with the state Islamic religious department, and the provision contains no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dress. A trans visitor who is Muslim therefore faces state Sharia exposure in Penang in addition to the federal offences; the Sharia enactment does not reach non-Muslims.

The most recent documented enforcement action in Penang in this record is a police raid on a male-only sauna in early December 2025, carried out days after the Home Minister publicly floated revisiting the relevant federal provisions. The record gives no arrest figures, charges, remand proceedings or outcome for that Penang raid. No subsequent Penang instance is documented.

Apart from that raid, no Penang-specific prosecution, court ruling or institutional practice is documented in the available sources. Human Rights Watch interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 for its report on conversion practices, discrimination and violence; interviewees lived in Penang, but the report records national-level patterns and contains no Penang-specific enforcement case. That research window closed in 2021.
tangentialFactors:
The Penang raid sits inside a documented escalation in operations against queer spaces elsewhere in Malaysia. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such operation since 2022, with detainees' faces and personal details leaked to pre-tipped media and 17 civil servants among those suspended; a magistrate rejected the remand extension for lack of ground, yet release was delayed. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later the Penang sauna was raided.

Venue raids elsewhere in the country provide the comparison set: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, an August 2022 raid on an LGBT venue in which twenty men were arrested, an October 2022 Queer Halloween party with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, and eleven shopping malls raided in May 2023 over Pride watches.

Other states have moved further by administrative and judicial route: a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and Johor approved plans for conversion-therapy centres in November 2023. These are other jurisdictions' practice, not Penang's.
localsOnly:
Penang's Islamic religious department is the enforcing body for the state Sharia enactment, which reaches Muslim residents only and criminalises cross-dressing alongside same-sex conduct, with penalties of up to three years, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. Officers exercise that discretion without a statutory definition of transgender dress.

Penang residents were among the 73 LGBT people interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2018–2021 research, published in August 2022 with Justice for Sisters, covering conversion practices, discriminatory treatment and violence against LGBT people in Malaysia. The report records national-level patterns and no Penang-specific case.
outOfScopeNotes:
Arrest figures, charges and court outcomes for the December 2025 Penang sauna raid are not sourced; the raid is recorded only as having occurred, so its scope and consequences remain unresolved.

Whether Penang's enactment is one of the three that also bar women from posing as men is unresolved in the available sources. Only the bar on Muslim men dressing as women is established as applying across all 13 states.

No prosecution under Penang's Sharia enactment, no Penang court ruling on gender identity or cross-dressing, and no Penang-specific discrimination or hate-crime case appear in the available sources. The Human Dignity Trust country profile last updated 16 December 2025 carries national material only and records no legal gender-recognition procedure for the country as a whole, a question the national record governs.
